design_detail: News & Views commentary in Nature Medicine (vol. 27, June 2021, pp. 950-951; published online 24 May 2021) by David J. Nutt and Harriet de Wit, written on the publication of the first phase 3 trial of MDMA-assisted therapy for severe PTSD (MAPP1; Mitchell et al., 2021) in the same issue. Eleven paragraphs of running text, one schematic figure (Fig. 1: the brain pathways of PTSD and the proposed site of action of MDMA in therapy; no data) and 12 references. No new data. The upper half of p. 950 carries the end of an unrelated News & Views (Furer, Kaushansky and Shlush, on 'CH' and inflammation), which was not used. The piece has no section headings, so paragraph numbers in the locators count its running-text paragraphs from the start (paragraphs 1-2 begin on p. 950, paragraphs 3-11 on p. 951).
can_establish: What two prominent psychopharmacologists argued when MAPP1 was published: how they read its significance, how they told the history of MDMA and its scheduling, which mechanisms they proposed for its effect in PTSD, and what they predicted and recommended.
cannot_establish: Whether MDMA-assisted therapy is effective or safe: the piece gives no number from the trial, does not appraise its design (comparator, blinding, expectancy, adverse-event recording), and its mechanistic account rests on studies of healthy volunteers and rodents.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (commentary). The trial discussed is described only as a phase 3 study in people with severe PTSD; no sample size is given.
sample.selection_effects: Citations are chosen to support the authors' reading: the trial, its sponsor's earlier phase 2 work, an open (uncontrolled) trial in alcohol use disorder, and mechanistic studies in healthy volunteers and rodents. No critical source is cited, and no source is given for the statements that historic fears about MDMA were overstated (p. 950) or that claims of brain damage were misleading (p. 951).

exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: As the commentary describes the trial's conditions: two or three MDMA doses given a few weeks apart within a structured psychotherapy programme, at what the authors call a relatively moderate dose; no amounts are given (p. 951, 7th and 10th paragraphs).

comparison.controls: Not applicable. The trial's comparison condition (placebo with the same therapy) is not described.

outcomes.instruments: None named: the commentary does not name the trial's primary outcome measure or report any result on it.
outcomes.operationalization: 'Significant efficacy', 'excellent safety profile', 'high efficacy' and 'similar tolerability profile' are used without definition or numbers.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not discussed: blinding, expectancy and functional unblinding are not mentioned.

analysis.effect_sizes: None. No sample size, effect size, interval, response or remission rate, or adverse-event count from the trial is reported.
analysis.selective_reporting: Only favourable aspects of the trial are mentioned; its limitations are not. The phase 3 trial is said to replicate phase 2 efficacy without noting that both came from the same sponsor's programme (MAPS), which the commentary itself describes (p. 951).

interpretation_gap.results_show: No data. The commentary's statements about the trial are summary judgments without numbers: significant efficacy, an excellent safety profile, replication of the high phase 2 efficacy with a similar tolerability profile, and no signs of tolerance or dependence after a few exposures.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The standfirst says only that MDMA 'may be a promising treatment' (p. 950), but the text goes further: it says approval now seems likely within a few years (p. 950), presents mechanisms taken from healthy-volunteer and rodent studies as a plausible account of the clinical effect, and argues for rescheduling (p. 951). It does not mention the comparison condition, blinding or expectancy, the sample size, how adverse events were collected, or the shared sponsorship of the phase 2 and phase 3 studies. The statement that there were no signs of tolerance or dependence rests on a regimen of a few supervised sessions, which cannot show the absence of dependence risk outside the trial. By August 2024 the FDA had rejected the application (Mahase, 2024).

timeline.event: Mithoefer et al. (2011), described in this commentary as the first clinical study of MDMA, in chronic, therapy-resistant PTSD (ref 3; not read).
MAPP1, the trial discussed here (Mitchell et al., 2021); read by the other first reader of this batch.
Matters Arising critique of MAPP1 (Halvorsen, Naudet and Cristea, 2021); not read for this card.
The trial authors' reply to the critiques (Mitchell, Coker and Yazar-Klosinski, 2021); not read for this card.
MAPP2, the second phase 3 trial (Mitchell et al., 2023).
The BMJ reports that the FDA rejected the sponsor's application and that three phase 2 analyses were retracted by Psychopharmacology (Mahase, 2024).

replication.where_it_stands: The authors' forecast that MDMA would probably be approved within a few years had not been borne out by August 2024, when the FDA rejected the application (Mahase, 2024). The commentary remains a record of how the first phase 3 trial was received by two prominent researchers; it adds no evidence on efficacy or harms.

funding.declared_conflicts: D.J.N. is a paid advisor to Awakn, a company with an interest in MDMA treatment research. No interests are listed for H. de Wit.
funding.affiliations_note: David J. Nutt: Division of Psychiatry, Imperial College London; Harriet de Wit: Department of Psychiatry and Behavioral Neuroscience, University of Chicago; the two contributed equally. Two of the 12 references are de Wit's own laboratory studies (refs 9 and 12, used for the mechanism); the reference list gives only first authors for most other entries, so further overlap with the authors' own work cannot be checked from it. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: For the claims this commentary makes: trials of MDMA-assisted therapy run independently of the sponsor, with a comparator that is harder to tell apart from MDMA, blinding and expectancy measured and reported, systematic recording of adverse events (including positive and abuse-related effects), and long-term follow-up; for dependence risk, follow-up of people treated outside trial conditions.

domains.note: A News & Views piece; no search, and citations chosen to support the narrative.
Neither the trial nor the phase 2 studies, the open alcohol trial or the healthy-volunteer studies are appraised.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: Two of 12 references are de Wit's own studies, used for the mechanism, not for the clinical claims.

Forecasts (approval within a few years), policy recommendations (rescheduling) and mechanistic proposals are presented alongside the trial result without distinguishing tested from hypothesized; safety is asserted without numbers.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence on the efficacy and safety of MDMA-assisted therapy (limitations of the trials and critical views under-represented)
domains.note: No limitation of the trial is mentioned; earlier concerns about harm are called mistruths and misleading claims without citation.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to commentaries (METHODS §5.3); the editors' narrative-review checklist is used. The piece may be cited for what two prominent researchers argued and predicted when MAPP1 was published, including their forecast of approval and their call for rescheduling. It is not evidence on efficacy, blinding, expectancy or adverse events, for which the trial reports themselves must be read.

key_findings.finding: The standfirst says the phase 3 study shows that MDMA may be a promising treatment for PTSD, requiring a shift in how the drug is perceived. The text describes MAPP1 as the first phase 3 study of MDMA, showing significant efficacy and an excellent safety profile in people with severe PTSD, and says it now seems likely that MDMA will be an approved medication in a few years.
key_findings.note: No numbers from the trial are given anywhere in the piece.

key_findings.finding: The authors state that most of the historic fears about MDMA, which had been branded a brain-damaging recreational drug, were overstated; no source is cited.

History as told by the authors: MDMA was invented by Merck in 1912 as a precursor in a synthesis of haemostatic substances (ref 2), tested by Merck in animals in 1927 and 1959, revived by Alexander Shulgin in the 1970s and used by therapists, notably in couples counselling; it was sold as 'ecstasy' and taken at raves; the US Drug Enforcement Administration, encouraged by what the authors call misleading claims of brain damage, criminalized it in 1985; therapists founded MAPS in 1986; by the end of the 1980s it was banned in most Western countries.
key_findings.locator: 2nd paragraph (p. 950, middle and right columns, continued on p. 951); 3rd and 4th paragraphs (p. 951, left column)
key_findings.note: The 1985 date differs from Madero and Alvarez (2023, p. 19), who date Schedule I classification to October 1986; see reporting issue 2.

key_findings.finding: The authors describe the Mithoefer team's study (ref 3, 2011) as the first clinical study of MDMA, showing remarkable efficacy in chronic, therapy-resistant PTSD; several phase 2 studies are said to have shown similar efficacy in similar patients, which led the FDA to grant Breakthrough Therapy designation to the MAPS programme, and the European Medicines Agency is said to have approved the protocol design for parallel phase 3 studies.
key_findings.locator: 5th paragraph (left column, continued in the middle column)

key_findings.finding: The phase 3 study is said to replicate the high efficacy seen in phase 2 trials (ref 3) with a similar tolerability profile; an open trial of MDMA for alcohol use disorder (ref 4) is said to have shown remarkably reduced drinking over 9 months; the authors expect approval for PTSD and alcohol use disorder, for use in specific psychotherapy settings with trained therapists, if follow-up studies replicate efficacy and the safety profile.

The authors call it remarkable that large clinical effects follow a small number of MDMA sessions within a structured psychotherapy programme, which they describe as a novel type of pharmacological intervention unlike any other in psychiatry.

Proposed pharmacology: MDMA resembles amphetamines but acts more on serotonin and is an agonist at the 5-HT2 family of receptors (ref 5); enhanced serotonergic function, directly or through oxytocin, may explain its empathogenic effects, and a rodent study suggests oxytocin may open a critical window for learning new behavioural responses (ref 6).

Proposed psychotherapeutic mechanism: MDMA facilitates exposure therapy by helping reactivate and then extinguish the emotional memory of the trauma (ref 7; Fig. 1); in healthy volunteers it reduces the impact of negative memories (refs 8, 9) and suppresses amygdala responses to negative stimuli (refs 9, 10), which the authors call a plausible mechanism; it also enhances social connection (refs 11, 12).
key_findings.locator: 9th paragraph (middle column, continued in the right column); Fig. 1 and legend (left column)
key_findings.note: Fig. 1 is a schematic with no data.

key_findings.finding: The authors write that mistruths about MDMA and its Schedule I classification fuel fears about harm and addictive potential and limit access, and that the trial supports the efficacy and safety of MDMA after a few exposures at what they call a relatively moderate dose, without signs of tolerance or dependence.

The authors call for MDMA to be rescheduled to a lower level of restriction in the UK and USA, which they say would greatly accelerate research and access, and for the World Health Organization and the United Nations to consider the same.
Competing interests: D.J.N. is a paid advisor to Awakn, a company with an interest in MDMA treatment research; nothing is listed for H. de Wit. Published online 24 May 2021.

reporting_issues.issue: The commentary reports no number from the trial it discusses: no sample size, outcome measure, effect size, interval, response or remission rate, or adverse-event count, so its characterizations (significant efficacy, an excellent safety profile, high efficacy, similar tolerability) cannot be checked against it.
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite the trial report, not this commentary, for any result.

reporting_issues.issue: The phase 3 study is said to replicate phase 2 efficacy; the commentary itself describes the phase 2 studies and the phase 3 programme as MAPS research, so the agreement is within one sponsor's programme, not an independent replication.
reporting_issues.consequence: Under METHODS §6.4 this would count at most as replication by the same team.

reporting_issues.issue: The commentary dates the criminalization of MDMA by the US Drug Enforcement Administration to 1985; Madero and Alvarez (2023, p. 19) date its Schedule I classification to October 1986. Neither cites a scheduling document.
reporting_issues.consequence: Dates of US scheduling should be taken from the legal-status sources (section 13), not from these commentaries.

reporting_issues.issue: The 2011 study by the Mithoefer team is called the first clinical study of MDMA, although the same piece describes Merck's animal tests and therapists' clinical use of MDMA in the 1970s and 1980s; the statement is unqualified and no earlier studies in people are discussed.
reporting_issues.consequence: Not to be cited for the history of clinical research with MDMA.

verification.source_read: PDF pp. 950-951 (PDFs/MDMA/Nutt_2021_PuttingMDBackIntoMDMA.pdf): the News & Views by Nutt and de Wit read in full, including Fig. 1 and its legend, the reference list, affiliations and the competing-interests statement; both pages rendered. The end of the preceding, unrelated News & Views on p. 950 was not used.
